newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban face pro-Rabbani forces north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Taleban face pro-Rabbani forces north of Kabul.

text.p: The Islamic Taleban movement consolidated its grip on the Afghan capital Kabul on Saturday, but made no attempt to advance north from the Bagram military airbase, witnesses said.
Four tanks flying the Taleban's plain white flag guarded the edge of the militia's territory at Bagram, 50 km (31 miles) north of the city.

A fighter confiscated a music cassette from a car passing the checkpost as part of a drive to enforce the Taleban's purist brand of Islam, but civilian traffic was flowing freely across the front line.
About 10 km (six miles) further up the road, a score of fighters loyal to deposed President Burhanuddin Rabbani manned a checkpoint just south of the town of Charikar, capital of Parwan province.

"The people of the Shomali valley (extending from north of Kabul to Salang) have decided to fight the Taleban wherever they are," said a young fighter named Mohammed Qassim, standing by an armoured personnel carrier with a red anti-tank rocket launcher mounted on top.
"We are fighting the Taleban because we gave sacrifices during the Russian invasion and we don't want to be expelled from our territory by the Taleban," said 20-year-old Abdul Waheed.

A Pakistan-based Afghan news service, the Afghan Islamic Press, earlier quoted Taleban sources as saying that the militia had captured Charikar. But witnesses said the town was still held by pro-Rabbani forces.
Taleban forces to the south were making no immediate preparations to thrust further north following their stunning takeover of Kabul on Friday from Rabbani's military commander Ahmad Shah Masood.

More than 30 vehicles, including tanks, armoured personnel carriers and trucks lay abandoned on the road north from Kabul, left behind by Masood's troops as they fled towards his stronghold of Jabal-us-Seraj at the foot of the Panjshir valley on Thursday night.

Some of the vehicles appeared to have broken down as they climbed the Khair Khana pass out of Kabul. The retreating troops had blown some of them up, reducing them to charred hulks with the gun turrets lying on the road.

At his command post in the village of Salang, just south of the Salang Tunnel, one of Masood's commanders blamed the loss of Kabul on a "conspiracy hatched by Pakistan's ISI (Inter-Services Intelligence), the CIA and the United Nations".

"They managed to buy off some local commanders and succeeded in bringing the war to the eastern edge of Kabul," General Basir, commander of the Salang highway sector, told reporters. "The war will not be over. We will start again."

He said Rabbani, Masood, Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar and Abdurrab Rasul Sayyaf, leader of a pro-Rabbani faction, were now all in the Panjshir Valley, the bastion of Masood's mainly ethnic Tajik forces.

Basir said he hoped northern militia leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who controls Masood's only supply line from the north, would ally with the former government or at least not cooperate with the Taleban.

The Taleban have previously spurned any accommodation with Dostum because of his past service with the former communist government of President Najibullah, who was summarily killed soon after the Islamic warriors entered Kabul and his body left hanging outside the presidential palace.

But Mullah Mohammad Rabbani, head of the Taleban's interim administration, told reporters on Friday that Dostum had now "shown himself to be a good Moslem" and had good relations with Kabul's new rulers.

Dostum commanders told Reuters in the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif on Thursday that their leader had ordered at least 40,000 troops to reinforce front lines against Taleban forces in the west and Masood's troops holding positions about 20 km (13 miles) north of the Salang tunnel.
"We will maintain our neutrality," said one commander. Dostum has not taken sides in the struggle pitting the Taleban against Rabbani and Masood.

Basir said several aircraft had been flown to the northern towns of Takhar and Kunduz before Bagram fell, but a Taleban commander said his fighters had found 25 planes there, including 18 Russian-made MiG fighters, when they captured the airbase without a battle on Friday.
"At first we thought it would be difficult because the government had such a big force," said Maulvi Akhtar Mohammad Mansoor. "But when we found the government isolated and fleeing, it became easy."
